ClientResponses.Response: Hi there, we’d like to provide some additional information about the shutdown process and help clarify what you experienced. When you select Shut Down, the hot rod can remain hot long enough to ignite the remaining pellets in the firepot until they turn to ash. This is expected, and the flame will eventually go out, which is why the lid should remain closed during the shutdown cycle. On WiFIRE enabled grills, it is also normal for the auger to continue feeding pellets into the firepot during shutdown. This is an intentional part of the design that helps prevent pellets remaining in the auger from catching fire. As the shutdown process continues, the auger will stop and the fan will continue running to complete the cycle. If you are referring to the auger continuously feeding pellets beyond the normal shutdown process, our support team can help determine what may be causing it and guide you through the appropriate next steps. You can also find helpful information for identifying continuous auger feeding here: https://support.traeger.com/hc/en-us/articles/4407213129115-Auger-Continuously-Feeding-Pellets. Traeger

ClientResponses.Response: Hello, and thank you for your feedback on the Pro 575. One thing that is not always realized about pellet grills is that they aren’t going to work like the older style stick smokers that many people are used to. One of the main differences is that they won't create plumes of dark, heavy smoke that constantly billows out of the grill and can add a bitter aftertaste to food, but rather are made to produce clean, thin “blue smoke”, which is the intentional goal of a Traeger, and all of the companies that copied the Traeger design. And while the benefit of cooking with blue smoke has been well documented in books, online and through other forms of media, the lack of visible exhaust can still create the impression that food really isn't getting smoked. But there are things you can do to increase the flavor even more if you aren't satisfied the current results. In addition to keeping the temperature at 225 degrees and lower for most of the cook (which is the ideal range for blue smoke production), you can also try placing the food on the upper rack where more smoke collects, as well as using butcher paper instead of aluminum foil to wrap meats to allow more smoke to penetrate. You might even experiment with different wood types to see what works best for you, with the single wood pellets often providing a more robust, unique flavor than blends. As for cooking in cold weather, although the Pro 575 is not one of our insulated models, such as the Timberline and Ironwood series, both of which also come with the Super Smoke feature, you can use an insulation blanket (just search for the item #: BAC626 on Traeger.com) for doing cooks under 350 degrees when the weather outside is below freezing. Not only will this improve the temperature management in the dead of winter, but it will also help the grill use less pellets as well.

As a previous Traeger owner, you are likely already aware that pellet grills are not big visual smoke producers, which is completely by design. When smoking food, dark, heavy, acrid smoke is never ideal, with thin blue smoke being much preferred for cooking. While the topic of blue smoke is well documented online, the method of increasing its production, and the resulting flavor, is not always as well known. The main approach, and one easily implemented on a pellet grill, is keeping the temperature low, preferably at 225 degrees or less, for most of the cook. Although visual smoke will still appear when the grill is first started, and briefly again whenever new pellets get added to the fire, the rest of the time you won’t see anything near as thick. However, even though this is actually the goal, it can create the impression that food isn’t getting properly smoked, sometimes to the point of altering our perception of the results. Results.ReviewText: Pro 575 maintains heat well. I haven't seen a big difference between my meater thermometer and the on board sensor.  Others have reported a large discrepancy but I didn't experience that. It disappointing that this model doesn't have a super smoke mode.  Even keeping temp below 225F doesn't provide the same flavor as the super smoke mode.  I've had to put a separate smoke canister inside. It's a pain but necessary to get flavor.  The hook the grease pail hangs on is poorly designed.  If you use a cover, the pail  falls when you remove the cover. I needed to design a latch that retains the pail. It could been designed a lot better without adding cost.  Hopper clean out is difficult as the door is behind the grill and the pellets do not free flow out of the hopper. A stick needs to be poked through the anger protection screen.  I'm sure that many people have just removed the screen.  The controller is easy to operate and the Mobil app screen is laid out well.  Cleaning the ash put requires all the heat shields and grates to be removed. Chamber cannot be removed and dumped, it has to be vacuumed.  Other competing grill have buckets that can be removed.  All in all, heat stability is good, controller is good but the pellet unloading process and ash pit cleaning ergonomics could be a lot better.  It a middle of the rode product at best.

ClientResponses.Response: Hi, and thanks for your feedback on the Pro 780. The cooking method by this model and earlier ones is really very much the same, so the outcome shouldn’t be that far off from what you’re used to. The Pro 780 cooks by burning the same wood pellets, in the same manner, as the Traegers that were made 15 or more years ago. And while cooking at temperatures of 225 and lower is definitely a great way to increase smoke flavor, there are a few other things you can try if the results still don’t meet your expectations. One is using the upper rack, if the grill has one installed. This will keep the meat closer to where the rising smoke collects than it would on the bottom rack (just watch your meat probe temps since it can also be a little hotter up there too). You might also consider using butcher paper instead of aluminum foil to wrap your food. Options like the Traeger Pink Butcher Paper are better at letting smoke through than foil, while still keeping food from drying out. Another idea is to experiment with different pellets, or at least make sure you are using the same wood type that you did with your earlier Traegers. Although all varieties should do a great job of adding flavor, some may be a little more robust, especially when referring to single wood types as opposed to the blends. And if you haven’t already, try taking a look at the different recipes at traeger.com/recipes. There you’ll find all sorts of ways to cook just about anything you can think of, and everything listed is specifically designed for doing on a Traeger just like yours.
